title: Asha Sharma-appointed Xbox VP of engineering leaves a mere three months after being moved over from Microsoft's CoreAI team
author: Sherif Saed
content:
Cognitive dissonance.

When Microsoft assigned Asha Sharma as the new leader of the Xbox division in February, replacing the Phil Spencer regime, the executive brought along some of her former colleagues with her. Now, one of those recent hires is leaving.

Jared Palmer, who previously held the title of Xbox VP of engineering, announced on X (via Kotaku) that he's joined Cognition, an AI company. "Personal update: I've joined Cognition to lead engineering," he wrote. "I'm grateful to Asha Sharma and everyone at Xbox for an amazing year."

Palmer was among several of Sharma's former colleagues at Microsoft's CoreAI team, which the executive brought to the Xbox team in May. At the time, she said Palmer will work on developer tools, engineering, product and infrastructure.

"He's spent his career building developer tools that remove friction and increase productivity," Sharma said of Palmer at the time. "That's exactly the mindset we want, using technology to support creators."

Palmer's stint at Microsoft as a whole has been brief, having joined CoreAI in October last year, before moving to the Xbox team seven months later. It's not clear what prompted the VP to leave after such a short period at Xbox, but the reason could have more to do with where he's going rather than anything to do with Microsoft.

Palmer leaves Xbox at the most tumultuous time in its history. As part of Asha Sharma's big reset plan, the executive laid off 1,600 people across almost all of the studios it owns, with further 1,600 to be laid off over the course of fiscal year 2027, for a total of 3,200. As part of the same campaign, Microsoft is divesting itself from four studios it previously owned, and is proposing the closure of another.

It's not clear what effect this is going to have on the future of the platform, particularly when it comes to Xbox's next-gen console Project Helix, as the year or so preceding a new console launch is typically when most of that platform work is concentrated.

title: Following layoffs and muddy strategy shifts, Xbox announces Backward Compatibility on PC program, with Blinx and Conker leading the first wave
author: Fran Ruiz
content:
Past distractions.

As Microsoft tries to downplay the effects on its gaming business of cutting 3,200 jobs and four studios, Xbox is rethinking its whole strategy even if the more recent comments from inside the house still sound confused at best. Don't worry though; old Xbox games are coming to PC.

Via Xbox Wire, the company has announced Xbox Backward Compatibility on PC, a surprise program that aims to bring 'classics' - more on this below - to PC and handhelds like the ROG Xbox Ally for the first time ever. The emulation effort also includes features like "graphics settings, including up to 4x resolution upscaling, VSync support, Fullscreen and Windowed display modes, anisotropic filtering, enhanced anti-aliasing, and more."

The first batch of games includes four oldies you may or may not have played before: Blinx: The Time Sweeper, Conker: Live and Reloaded, Crimson Skies: High Road to Revenge, and Fuzion Frenzy. Though there are very vocal voices out there when it comes to gassing up games like Crimson Skies, these aren't system sellers. Still, we have to respect the effort, especially at a time when everyone is selling remakes and remasters while making old releases hard to buy and play. Earlier this generation, Xbox's backwards compatibility project was one of the brand's biggest strengths, so it's nice to see it revived and evolved in some way.

According to the announcement, "each of these games is now available for purchase on PC and also included with all Xbox Game Pass plans", with the separate purchase prices sitting at $9.99 (regional prices may vary). "If you already own a digital license for these games on console, that license now carries over to your PC or handheld," so that's also neat. They have cloud support, too.

"We plan to add even more features to Xbox Backward Compatibility games in the future," Jason Ronald, VP of next generation at Xbox, teased. In fact, these first four games will get achievements in the coming months. The sudden and half-baked nature of this first wave makes me think that, even if the push is well-meaning, this is another "break in case of emergency" fast reveal, like last week's Bethesda roadmap.

It's unclear if this move signals a return to the backwards compatibility efforts for Xbox consoles as well, but it's certainly a step in the right direction. Elsewhere, it's unclear if Sony's PlayStation 6 will even have a disc drive to play games from previous generations after it was revealed the company would drop physical game releases entirely starting in 2028. Platforms like GOG are still trying to fight to preserve all sorts of games, though.

title: Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 confirms release date and it's closer than you think
author: Vikki Blake
content:
Planet now.

Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2 will release on 25th August 2026.

Details of an unannounced Aliens: Fireteam Elite sequel popped up as early as July 2024, when a pitch deck detailing "a new chapter in the Aliens: Fireteam Elite" series leaked online. At that time, it was expected to launch by Q3 2025.

Then, in May, the game was finally confirmed, only this time with a release window of Q3 2026 instead.

In an extraordinarily brief, action-packed, and thoroughly gore-soaked teaser, Cold Iron revealed the release date and teased "new perks, abilities, weapons, Xenomorphs, and more".

ICYMI, the sequel expands from three-player co-op to four players, as well as "deeper strategies and smoother coordination with your squad, [with] a variety of new classes and weapons each bringing unique playstyles and tactical possibilities to the battlefield".

Other features include an updated horde mode, a new Specialist endgame class for fully custom Marines, five unique classes, and "deadlier threats". Players will also be able to team up cross-platform with in-game voice chat. It's coming to PC via Steam and Epic Games Store, as well as the PS5 and Xbox Series X/S.

"Aliens: Fireteam Elite is exactly what it says on the tin. Stuffed with guns, gadgets, and plentiful alien goo, it's a frenetic cooperative firefight against some of sci-fi's most iconic monsters in an all-new tale that takes us beyond the original trilogy," I wrote when I reviewed Aliens: Fireteam Elite back in 2021.

"No, it's not the most sophisticated shooter, and no, its truncated runtime is unlikely to occupy you for more than a couple of nights, but it's an unashamedly good romp that'll hopefully satisfy your Ripley power fantasies, too."

title: What are we all playing this weekend?
author: James Archer
content:
Well? Do tell!

I spent most of last Saturday laid out in a Baku hotel room, muscles in both legs ground to flecks of useless meat by the decision to walk down a mountain when there was a perfectly good funicular right there. May this weekend be more fruitful, and less marred by the stupidity of trying to please a step counter that only truly cares about where its next battery charge is coming from. Ruinous silicone bastard.

Edwin: After writing about Star Wars: Zero Company this week I feel a hankering for a tactics RPG of some kind. Perhaps I'll dig out that Troubleshooter: Abandoned Children game you're all so keen on, or maybe I will fire up Othercide on the Switch (assuming the interface, which I recall being torturous on PS4, transfers easily to the smaller screen). Beyond that, I've just bought a new poetry tome, Aaron Kent's Angels the Size of Houses.

Jeremy: This weekend I'll either be chugging along with Black Flag Resynced or maybe returning to Lords of the Fallen, which got put on the backburner after I decided to be a pirate for a bit rather than an emo goth knight wandering through a depressing world where everything's gone to shite. Speaking of post-apocalyptic worlds, there's also another secret game along these lines that I'll be firing up for guides prep sometime soon. Look to the release schedule in August for possible hints, I say!

James: I slapped Replaced on my Steam Deck last week for the pre-muscledeath plane trip, then spent the whole flight in Silksong instead. What can I say, I can’t get enough bug gibberish. I should play Replaced more, though.

Ollie: Sorry, the bargo gods hath sewn shut my mouth.

Mark: I've been thinking I might finally get around to trying Assassin's Creed Rogue. It's the entry that followed on from the recently resynced Black Flag and attempted to build on the naval battles I loved in that game, but I've never gotten around to giving it a go. It's not unique in that regard, I've missed a number of AC entries in the years since Black Flag, specifically Valhalla, Origins and Syndicate. I should also really get around to finishing the remastered version of Assassin's Creed 3 after starting it about half a decade ago. God, there are just so many games about people in hoodies jumping around.

Julian, Dion, and Callum do not recognise the the weekend's claim to the end of the week.

And you, reader dear, what are you playing this weekend?...

title: Trump Plans to Impose New Illegal Tariffs on Canada
author: IlyaSomin
content:
Today, Donald Trump announced plans to impose 50% tariffs on a wide range of Canadian imports to the United States:

President Trump is imposing 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods, from hockey equipment to alcoholic beverages, escalating the trade dispute between the two countries.

The new tariffs — laid out in a series of proclamations signed by Mr. Trump on Monday — are set to take effect on Aug. 19. The White House accused Canada of "unreasonable, unequal, and discriminatory actions" by imposing tariffs or import restrictions on certain American goods, some of which began after Mr. Trump's initial round of tariffs on Canada last year.

In retaliation for last year's Canadian tariffs on certain U.S. auto imports, the Trump administration slapped tariffs on certain Canadian electronics, hockey equipment, honey, flower bulbs, down feathers, plywood, cowhides, jewelry and other goods. The White House also imposed tariffs on Canadian beer, wine, liquor and milk, in response to Canadian boycotts of U.S. alcohol in response to last year's tariffs and longstanding Canadian quotas on dairy imports.

Goods that flow across the border under the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement, or USMCA — a trade deal inked during Mr. Trump's first term — will not be exempt from the new tariffs, a senior administration official told reporters Monday.

The new tariffs are based on Section 338 of the notorious 1930 Smoot-Hawley tariff legislation, which severely exacerbated the Great Depression. As Philip Zelikow of the conservative Hoover Institution explained in a guest post here at the VC blog, last year, Section 338 was long-ago superseded by new legislation enacted in 1962 and 1974, and is therefore defunct. For that reason, it has not been used since at least the 1940s.

Georgetown University trade policy scholar Peter Harrell summarizes additional useful points about the new tariffs on Twitter, including some additional legal objections to them. Should the new tariffs come into effect, there will likely be legal challenges, and those challenges will richly deserve to prevail.

I would add that this is just the latest of a series of efforts by Trump to usurp congressional tariff authority and impose harmful and dangerous trade restrictions that damage the US economy and poison relations with our allies and trading partners, of which Canada is one of the most important. That includes the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) tariffs struck down by the Supreme Court in February, in a case I helped bring, the  Section 122 tariffs  invalidated by the US Court of International Trade, his massive planned Section 301 tariffs, and - most recently - his threat to impose tariffs on Canada in response to wildfires there. Courts should continue to reject these dangerous power grabs and affronts to the rule of law.

I may well have more to say about these new tariffs later, especially if they end up getting implemented, as currently planned.

title: Does This Photo from the Curiosity Rover Prove an Intense Sandstorm on Mars?
content:
The Curiosity rover has been trundling over the red rocks and sand of Mars since August 2012, and it continues to make fascinating discoveries.

Featured Video

In fact, it just uncovered evidence of a Martian sandstorm that lasted for hours and happened billions of years ago—the first direct physical evidence of such an event on the planet that we’ve found so far.

What Curiosity spotted was ripples on ripples: Sand pushed so hard by the wind that the ripples are climbing over each other. These layers then hardened into rock over eons, leaving behind the geological patterns shown in this image, snapped by Curiosity on Dec. 12, 2024 in the Gale crater.

Read more: “Hear the Wind on Mars”

An interpretation of these patterns, more technically known as supercritical climbing translatent strata, has now been published in a study in Geology. Using the angles and volumes that sediment was deposited in, scientists can work backward to figure out the wind conditions at the time.

“These conditions caused rapid deposition of sediment onto migrating wind ripples, occasionally resulting in supercritical angles of climb, recording gusting winds that originated from the south,” write the researchers.

The analysis floats two hypotheses to fit the data: Either the sand grains were forced up dune and rock edges before falling over and accumulating, or they were being pushed down a slope with slight imperfections in the terrain, causing ripples to build up. The fact that these “climbing” ripples are interspersed with more ordinary, flat wind ripples suggests intense bursts of wind that came and went, giving us invaluable insight into meteorological conditions on the Red Planet billions of years ago that could help us understand more about what led to its current state.

“These are the shortest duration fluctuations in wind speed identified for ancient Mars thus far, recording extremely transient atmospheric conditions during a time when the Martian climate was becoming increasingly arid,” write the researchers.

The thinking is that while Mars was once home to a vast network of rivers and oceans, its surface has now been dry for several billion years—with solar winds stripping liquid off the planet, left vulnerable by a weakening magnetic field.

As Curiosity will be experiencing (and anyone who’s seen The Martian knows), there are still large, intense dust storms on Mars today. They can be the size of continents—big enough to be seen from Earth, via telescope—and last for weeks. Every three Mars years or so, one gets big enough to envelope the entire planet. Now we can start to compare those conditions to ancient Mars, through a reverse weather forecast stretching over billions of years.

title: How Bots Took Over Our Lives
author: @NewYorker
content:
During the 2016 election, much of the country was introduced to the concept of internet bots for the first time. Now, just a decade later, it feels like they’re everywhere.

July 27, 2026

Photograph by Vincent Forstenlechner / Connected Archives

All the way back in 2016, when Donald Trump won his first Presidential election, many people had trouble understanding how, exactly, it could have happened. The line of inquisition extended to the political class, where recriminations from talking heads on MSNBC about Hillary Clinton’s ineffective campaigning and tone-deaf messaging abounded. Others, though, gravitated toward a more sinister conspiracy, which involved foreign interference and a network of automated agitators spreading disinformation at scale. The bots, this emerging coalition said, were to blame for Trump’s rise.

During the past decade, so-called bots, a slippery concept from the start, have gone from a conspiratorial curiosity to a familiar force in our daily lives. In the popular imagination, they are suddenly everywhere and seem designed to annoy the hell out of people. Consider the familiar indignity of buying concert tickets only to find that, immediately after a sale opens, every ticket has been purchased by an army of bots, only to be listed on a resale site with a markup of hundreds or even thousands of dollars. This is their function: bots operate on a scale and speed that gives them an unfair advantage over humans, who have to fumble around with mouse clicks and thoughts. They hoard inventory on e-commerce sites to frustrate customers and torture retailers, and scan real-estate websites so they can send automated text messages to homeowners with lowball offers. They trawl the internet to scrape e-mail addresses and then fill inboxes with phishing attempts and spam.

But the impulse to treat bots like digital mosquitoes that need to be swatted away minimizes their role in making the internet work. At their most basic, bots are bits of programming built to run a certain function automatically until something or someone stops them. They are tools, and as much as general attitudes toward them have become negative they are most often used for mundane tasks. Still, our reflexive reaction to bots on social media is irritation and suspicion—to call something a “bot” is to label it as unthinking and nonhuman. That instinct partly originated in the blame game following Clinton’s narrow loss in the 2016 election, with the rise of a general if somewhat vague consensus that a web of coördinated political agitators based in Russia had used social-networking sites like Facebook and Twitter to sow disorder and distrust in the American electorate.

The accusation wasn’t without merit. Following Trump’s victory, the Internet Research Agency, a St. Petersburg-based “troll farm,” was accused of interfering in American elections, a detail revealed in the Mueller report. According to the report, the I.R.A. had been planning this digital-agitprop campaign for several years prior to the election, even travelling to the U.S. to take photos to use in their posts. They deployed bots to pose as American grassroots political organizers, eventually making virtual contact with Trump supporters and campaign officials, and to spread bogus headlines targeted at voters in swing states. According to the report, the I.R.A.’s strategy evolved from a generalized attempt to destabilize American politics to, per the report, “a targeted operation that by early 2016 favored candidate Trump and disparaged candidate Clinton.”

This meant that the disappointed liberals who had grown convinced that Russia tilted the election toward Trump were right—or at least half right. The degree to which the Russian efforts were effective is still an open question, and some reports have cast doubt on social media’s ability to drive political outcomes. A study published in 2023 by N.Y.U.’s Center for Social Media and Politics, in Nature Communications, found that Russian bots on Twitter had limited influence, with one per cent of users being exposed to seventy per cent of the posts created by Russian troll accounts. There was also a study conducted by professors at Dartmouth, Princeton, and the University of Exeter in 2017 which found that the majority of “fake news” promoted on sites like Facebook was being consumed by hard-line conservatives who likely would have voted for Trump anyway. But it didn’t matter. The Mueller report and the spectre of Russian influence provided an easy answer for a stunning political defeat, and the modern mythology of the bots was born.

In the years since 2016, bot networks have become only more sophisticated, and the proliferation of A.I. technology promises to widen their scope. Analysis from the internet-infrastructure giant Cloudflare estimates that nearly sixty per cent of internet traffic is nonhuman. In practice, that means that many exchanges on the internet are just bots talking to other bots in an automated loop. Years ago, as virtual assistants were first taking off, a video recording of what happened when a human asked two Alexa-equipped devices at the same time to start a psychotherapy session. They end up in an infinite recursion of questions without making any progress. Now imagine that process scaled up to the size of the internet, and you have an approximation of the bot-saturated social-media platforms. Researchers at one A.I. company estimated that of a sample of more than a million accounts on X, sixty-four per cent could be bots, a finding that requires no stretch of the imagination, given the sheer inanity of interactions on the site. Under any number of viral posts, you can find accounts responding with a sequence of increasingly brainless rehashings of the original content, like a series of photocopies that slowly deteriorate in quality.

The quantity of bots on Twitter was a key sticking point for Elon Musk during his purchase of the company in 2022, and his subsequent, unsuccessful attempt to back out of the deal. He estimated that twenty per cent of the site was made up of automated accounts, a dynamic that had overvalued Twitter and should therefore allow him to walk away from his hasty acquisition. Twitter, at that point, claimed that the ratio was closer to five per cent. But bots aren’t just sitting around talking to each other; they are also a major factor in what posts become popular, facilitating virality by clustering around certain subjects and liking and reposting specific posts, creating a flywheel of engagement that spreads whatever message someone might be amplifying.

This strategy of manufacturing a froth of interest around a given subject, from Nicki Minaj’s political perspectives to Sydney Sweeney’s jean ads, has recently been especially effective, and has moved culture-war fights from the trenches of bot-infested social networks into more mainstream channels. A New York Times investigation into the social media fracas found that there were relatively few mentions of Sweeney on X until several days after the début of her infamous American Eagle commercial, and less than ten per cent of those early posts were directly critical. It wasn’t until a couple of posts that compared the ad to Nazi eugenics propaganda ended up going viral that the outrage cycle began, and conservative influencers attempted to paint what was essentially a fringe perspective on the ad campaign as a liberal consensus.

“These episodes follow a common pattern: a small incident is framed as ‘proof’ of a broader culture war, then a mix of real users, coördinated accounts, and bots push the same talking points and narratives until it looks like a widespread response,” Emilio Ferrara, a computer-science professor at U.S.C., told me. Extreme voices with high follower counts, such as Chaya Raichik, the woman behind the right-wing X account Libs of TikTok, are usually at the center of the skirmish, and then bot networks swarm to boost the message. It’s like pouring gasoline onto a few embers, which then appears to be a bonfire. Lynnette Ng, a former bot-network researcher at Carnegie Mellon University, explained why the swarm is so effective: “Bots frequently and aggressively hit cognitive-bias triggers in their messages which push the brain to short-circuit people’s ability to reason about the information in front of them.” It doesn’t help that people struggle to decipher bots from humans in the first place during political conversations. The default heat setting for political discourse online is already so high that it tends to pressurize such conversations into a single, highly combustible layer. Bots that are designed to inflame those political disagreements are trained on those conversations and then injected back into the discourse, amplifying the feedback loop of people yelling at bots who are yelling at people, and so on.

This is easy enough to understand; bots are like automated moths to digital flame. But the rationale propelling them is a little harder to decipher. Surely, some of the motive is financial, as engagement on social-media platforms has been monetized. On X, for example, an account is able to participate in X’s revenue-sharing program as long as it is “verified”—which really just means that the owner has paid a small fee for a premium account—and the page meets minimum metrics such as having five hundred verified followers and a certain number of recent “organic” impressions. (“Organic” here means that you didn’t pay for your posts to be promoted like an ad.) There’s no quality incentive here; as long as a post is attracting eyeballs and generating ad impressions, there is a potential for payout. A bot that is programmed to maximize engagement and to interact with accounts that have lots of followers can make money for its operator by appearing next to ads in the X timeline. A.I. has made that feedback loop spin only faster: bots now learn what sort of content drives the most engagement and adjust their outputs to generate likes, reposts, and comments.

Unfortunately, the posts that get the most engagement are invariably the ones that upset us the most. Rage-baiting, as this strategy is often called, is an effective behavior to program into a bot’s temperament, since people are more likely to engage with social-media posts that challenge their beliefs than those that confirm them. Maintaining a system powered by invective discourse also seems to be a practical business model for social-media platforms. A group of researchers found that removing toxic posts from a user’s feed reduced the amount of time they spent on a given platform. The total time that users spend mindlessly scrolling is the lifeblood of social-media outlets, meaning, as Ferrara explained, that they are dealing with a “conflicting system of incentives,” since bots are good for engagement metrics that can be attractive to advertisers but also mar user experience past a certain threshold. Keeping things just toxic enough so that users scroll without getting too upset at the state of the world is the sweet spot for platforms. It’s cynical, but it’s also very good business.

The platform engineers who keep people scrolling are only one cog in the attention-capturing machine. The people who create and deploy bot networks are pulling another set of levers in their attempt to make money or influence public opinion, and conflict is very good at attracting eyeballs. Many bots on social media are trained to maximize engagement, and the number of likes, shares, or comments a post receives is a large component of how the algorithms on X, Instagram, and TikTok decide what to put in front of users next. Those two parties—the platform owners who tweak the algorithm’s currents and the bot operators who ride it—work in tandem to shape people’s experiences online and end up warping reality in the process. There’s a growing weariness about the bot-dominated internet, though. Perhaps it explains why so many people were upset when it was revealed that Geese, a band beloved by the exact kinds of people who consider their music taste to be unassailably authentic, had reportedly worked with a marketing company to create legions of fake fan accounts. This tactic is not a major deviation from decades of creative and manipulative music marketing, but coverage of the controversy was overwhelmingly negative. Critics accused the band’s label of waging a “PsyOp,” one in which bots were capable of building an alternate reality and tricking them into liking something, almost against their will.

Ng compared the mechanics behind the glut of bots inflaming culture-war topics to an automated propaganda war that is currently being won by the individuals and groups more willing to use available technologies to pursue their own ends. “They’re an interesting tool for automated advertising that can be used by people to do good and do harm. Instead of us focussing on bots that are doing harm, we should focus on how we can use the same technology to make them do good.” It’s a pragmatic solution, if a little depressing, to give over the rest of the internet to automated skirmishes against disinformation.

Personally, I’d rather let the bots fight one another and log off forever. And yet the bot revolution is coming—or is perhaps already here—whether we like it or not. It goes far beyond political discourse, as bots now dominate how we experience life online: the customer-support chatbots that pop up when you want to rebook a flight, A.I.-powered summaries at the top of Google searches, automatic censors that flag and remove explicit content. But what happens when bots are all that’s left of digital life? Such a reality doesn’t seem terribly far away. Some in Silicon Valley would hand their entire lives over to “agents,” a dressed-up term for bots which has become one of the industry’s favorite words. Agents, though, are conceived of as independent and capable of reasoning, a spin along the lines of “bots with thoughts.”

In February, a security researcher at Meta named Summer Yue created an A.I. agent using the platform OpenClaw that she tasked with managing her Gmail account and suggesting which messages she should delete. Before she knew it, the bot started deleting all the e-mails in her inbox, like a digital locust. “I couldn’t stop it from my phone. I had to RUN to my Mac mini like I was defusing a bomb,” she wrote on X. That a security researcher for Meta was comfortable handing over the keys to her e-mail account to an autonomous bot that quickly went feral was funny, but after reading Yue’s story I found myself staring at my inbox. It was Sunday afternoon, and I had just got back from a weekend away. The number of unread e-mails in my inbox hovered around eighty thousand, and I found myself fantasizing about turning my whole life over to the bots and letting an agent nuke my overflowing inbox. It sounded liberating. Perhaps that’s what the A.I. apocalypse is really shaping up to be—not the elimination of humanity by an omniscient machine mind but an internet overrun by unthinking, error-prone automatons that make the web unusable and destroy it from the inside. After the bots take over, we can all get back to the real world. ♦

title: Amazon’s trying to launch a global satellite cellphone network in 2028
author: Stevie Bonifield
content:
Stevie Bonifield

is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Amazon filed an FCC application on Saturday to launch a new Leo satellite constellation that will provide direct-to-device satellite service for “voice, messaging, data, and emergency services.” If approved, Amazon will begin deploying the new constellation of 5,105 satellites in 2028. It says it plans to partner with mobile network operators to offer direct-to-device satellite service, similar to Starlink’s partnership with T-Mobile.

Earlier this year, Amazon announced it’s acquiring Globalstar’s satellite network and taking over its deal to provide direct-to-device satellite services for Apple devices. Amazon says its new constellation will “use Globalstar’s spectrum,” adding that it plans to “collaborate with Apple on future satellite services using the expanded network.” Advanced Television points out that the FCC application also includes a request to use spectrum assigned to Iridium’s satellite network outside the US, even as Rocket Lab is in the process of acquiring Iridium with plans to expand.

The new constellation and direct-to-device service will “complement” the broadband services Amazon also plans to offer through its Leo platform. In addition to consumer satellite service, it would also be used for things like disaster response and emergency messaging.

Amazon says the new direct-to-device satellites “will process the signals in orbit before relaying them to improve performance.” The new constellation will be nearly double the size of Amazon’s initial Leo constellation, which is planned to include around 3,200 satellites. As of July 2nd, Amazon says “over 375” of those satellites have launched so far.

title: Terrific castle-building sim Cataclismo is being transformed into a chunky strategy boardgame, care of a paid Old Kingdom expansion
author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
content:
Out 20th August

Excellent real-time castle defender Cataclismo is getting a DLC expansion, The Old Kingdom, which transforms it into a hex-based strategy boardgame. Players must hexpand from citadel to citadel, shoring up supply lines and unlocking technology while fending off the minions of the Mist. Please aim your Lobbers and Cannoneers at this trailer.

It's sort of the Cataclismo equivalent of Darkest Dungeon 2's Kingdoms mode, unfolding on a papery war table with books and playing pieces. And it goes hand-in-hand with that good, good block-building functionality that drove a gesticulating Nic Reuben (RPS in peace) to write about staircases in language more befitting of Lumiere the Candlestick singing about table service.

Speaking of language, I should disclose that former RPS contributor Brendy wrote words for Cataclismo. My writing words about his words represents a potential conflict of interest, but please rest assured that I loathe Brendy, co-founder of diseased internet hovel Jank.cool, and have many times generously invited him to go jump in the sea.

Anyway, back to The Old Kingdom. To spell it out a little, this appears to be the classic Total War split between a turn-based overworld and real-time clashes on the ground. Publishers Hooded Horse offer this summary:

"Venture forth to reclaim a lost kingdom in a new strategic game mode where players must expand their domain through multiple citadels, growing the realm’s economy and military might turn by turn. Manage and dispatch troops between sites, sending crucial reinforcements to vulnerable points and delivering vital supplies to where they’re needed most. Build up defenses across multiple fortresses to hold back the onslaught of horrors from the Mist, which grow stronger with each passing day. Unlock vital technologies that enable powerful abilities that will help win the ultimate victory!"

We never got round to doing a full review of Cataclismo, but not for want of enjoyment. Here is a representative excerpt from Nic's wallgasm: "The RTS-meets-tower-defence of its wave survival is sturdy and satisfying; its economic management tense and fraught with tight calls." The Old Kingdom expansion will launch on PC via Steam, GOG, the Epic Games Store, and the Microsoft Store on August 20th.

title: If you miss the straightforward action RPGs of the past, try the generous demo for Darkstone Restoration
author: Jody Macgregor
content:
Before action RPGs relied on seasonal ladders and DLC treadmills there was Darkstone, a 1999 hack and slash where you clicked on things until they died and liked it. It had some interesting ideas, like the companion mode that lets you switch between two player-characters, the other controlled by the CPU while you took the lead, but it remained true to the basics of a genre I got into precisely because it was basic.

Now it's back, with a remaster in early access that improves the UI and controls (you can move characters with WASD now, or play with a controller), and the graphics (though I had to turn off volumetric fog and procedural grass for the sake of my poor framerate).

It's got a demo too, which lets you make characters from any of its eight classes and explore the early-game dungeons, letting you play three of its quests, which are selected at random each time you start a new game.

It's just nice to start up an action RPG without having to worry about which build I'm going to pursue, or look at a massive node full of future skill unlocks, or wonder if I should start a seasonal character or whether I'm missing out by not buying the latest DLC. Darkstone is just Darkstone, a game of clicking on skeletons and goblins until they die, and as that annoying guy who though the first Diablo was the best Diablo it's really scratching the itch.

I want an action RPG that understands these are games I play when I need a break from thinky puzzly heavy games and want something light and, you know, more action-packed. I'll get back into them later, right now I really want to fight some giant wasps in a hole in the ground. Darkstone Restoration is perfect for that.

The only notable thing missing from the early access build is online multiplayer, though it does have couch co-op. A permadeath mode is also in the works. You can download the demo on Steam.
